newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-EMU prospects brighten as Bonn bows on jobs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EMU prospects brighten as Bonn bows on jobs.

text.p: The prospects for European economic and monetary union (EMU) brightened on Wednesday as Germany appeared to take steps to avert any collision over the single currency with the new Socialist-led government in Paris.

Days after the spectre of a new clash between Paris and Bonn over a stability pact cast doubt over the timetable for monetary union, both countries seemed ready to compromise to salvage the deal at next week's European Union summit.

Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, bowing to French insistence that job creation should be at the heart of EU policy, pledged support for putting an Employment Chapter in the Maastricht Treaty as long as it did not entail costly public job schemes.

"We do not want any unaccountable, unfinanceable or expensive spending programmes," he said. "Improved coordination of national measures at European level can take us further. On these terms, the government will agree to a jobs chapter."

France's new finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn stunned his European partners on Monday when he announced that Paris was not yet able to give final approval to the stability pact, which is aimed at ensuring budget discipline among nations joing the single currency.

France wants to shift the focus of monetary union away from a Bundesbank-led orientation on price stability to what it says is a return to the original balance between monetary discipline and economic growth and jobs struck between Paris and Bonn

Bonn must insist on strict monetary discipline in order to convince wary Germans to give up their beloved Deutschemark for an uncertain euro and has opposed any European spending spree on job schemes that could bloat budget deficits.
Hoping to salvage the stability pact and the EMU timetable, European politicians have been scrambling to find some form of compromise that could bring Paris and Bonn back together.

These diplomatic efforts appeared to be bearing fruit as statements from European capitals on Wednesday raised the possibilty that Paris could still approve the stability pact at the EU summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.
"We are clearly going to find a solution," Strauss-Kahn said in Paris after the weekly cabinet meeting. "The question is to know how to obtain the balance we are seeking."
Kinkel and several other European politicians sought to correct the view that France had cooled on monetary union.

European Commission President Jacques Santer, after meeting Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok and French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, told a news conference in Strasbourg he expected the EU summit in Amsterdam to approve the stability pact.
"From what I know as a result of the meeting with Wim Kok and Jospin ... it would seem based on these discussion we can succeed in Amsterdam," he said.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and a chorus of German politicians dismissed calls from some corners to delay monetary union.
"We will make the necessary decisions based on the criteria in the Maastricht Treaty within the prescribed timetable and launch the euro," Kohl said.
"Anything else would have catastrophic consequences for the German economy, a catastrophic impact on the labour market, for our currency and others."

Despite the German government's gestures towards Paris over an employment chapter, rumblings from within the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) indicated that Bonn will not be able to bend too far.

The CSU, a core part of the German coalition government, made clear it would tolerate no loosening of any element of monetary union and asserted itself as Europe's most vocal political force behind a "hard" EMU.

"Economic and monetary union begins on January 1, 1999 as a community of stability or it must be postponed and that means until the conditions are met," said Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, a staunch Euro-sceptic.

As the EMU debate continued, Kohl's beleaguered coalition came no closer to healing the strains that have arisen between Kohl's Christian Democrats and the Free Democrats over tax reform and yawning budget deficits.
The opposition Social Democrats said they might drop their rejection of the government's planned tax reforms if a partial shakeup of the tax system is brought into force this October.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150
